description:
Hello from Uruguay! 🇺🇾🚀

We are F.B.I., a team of students from Santa Elena School in Uruguay, excited to participate in the NASA Space Apps Challenge! 🌎✨
summary: This device is a smart temperature control system for spacecraft cabins, created by Alina, Emilia, Ema and Paulina, four 11- and 12-year-old students from Santa Elena School in Uruguay. Using a BBC micro:bit, the system measures the temperature several times per second and shows it on a small screen. If the temperature rises above 25 °C, a fan turns on automatically to cool the cabin, and it turns off when the temperature goes back down. Astronauts can also switch to manual mode and control the fan with a button. In space, there is no natural airflow, so spacecraft depend on machines to keep the air comfortable and safe for the crew. Our project shows, on a small scale, how technology can help protect astronauts’ health and comfort, and it is the first step toward a system that could also monitor body temperature and heart rate.
details:
What it does and how it works. The micro:bit, connected to an Sensor:bit board, works as the brain of the system. It reads the temperature several times per second and decides what to do. An OLED screen shows the current temperature and whether the fan is on or off. A DC motor with a propeller works as the fan.

Two modes:

  1. Automatic mode: if the temperature is above 25 °C, the fan turns on; at 25 °C or lower, it turns off.
  2. Manual mode: each press of the crash sensor turns the fan on or off.

Pressing buttons A and B at the same time switches between the two modes.

Benefits and intended impact. The system keeps the environment comfortable automatically, so astronauts can focus on their work, while still letting them take control when they need to. The same idea could be used on Earth in classrooms, homes or greenhouses.

Tools used. BBC micro:bit, Elecfreaks Sensor:bit board, OLED screen, DC motor with propeller, crash sensor, rainbow LED, and Microsoft MakeCode for programming. The presentation was made in Canva.

Creativity. We designed a system with both automatic and manual control, because astronauts need technology that works on its own but that they can also override.

Factors we considered and next steps. We discovered that the micro:bit measures the temperature of its own chip, which can read a few degrees higher than the air. Our next steps are to add a more accurate temperature sensor and a heart rate sensor, so the screen can also show the astronaut’s pulse and body temperature.
dataRefs: NASA: Wearable Tech for Space Station Research
NASA Environmental Control and Life Support Systems (ECLSS)
